policy_title: Support marriage through the tax system

verdict.plain: This policy would let married couples transfer up to 25% of one spouse's personal allowance to the other, saving higher-earning partners up to around £1,000 a year in tax — a real but modest gain for a subset of married couples. The big caveat is that it only helps couples where one earns below the personal allowance threshold, and some would gain far less due to interactions with benefits and tax credits.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether the policy is ever enacted — the 'as soon as finances allow' conditionality means there is no committed delivery date — and whether low historical take-up of the existing allowance would limit real-world gains.

claims.claim: The policy would allow a spouse to transfer 25% of their personal allowance to their partner, so neither pays tax on the first £25,000 of income.
claims.quote: introduce a UK 25% transferable marriage tax allowance as soon as finances allow, meaning no tax on the first £25,000 of income for either spouse

claims.claim: The current marriage allowance only permits transfer of 10% of the personal allowance (£1,260), saving the receiving partner up to £252 per year.
claims.quote: This transfer reduces the higher-earner's tax bill by up to £252 per year (20% of £1,260)

claims.claim: Under the proposed 25% transferable allowance, the maximum saving for the receiving partner would rise to around £1,000 per year.
claims.quote: This would result in a tax saving of up to £1,000 per year for the receiving partner (20% of £5,000), a significant increase from the current £252

claims.claim: Currently only around 3.9 million out of 12.4 million married or civil partnered couples benefit from the existing allowance.
claims.quote: roughly 3.9 million out of 12.4 million married or civil partnered couples benefit, with around 2.7 million being in-work couples

claims.claim: A more generous transferable allowance is described by the IFS as notable but dwarfed in size by the accompanying personal allowance increase.
claims.quote: a "more generous transferable marriage tax allowance" is a notable giveaway, it is "dwarfed in size" by the proposed increase in the Personal Allowance

claims.claim: Around two-fifths of eligible in-work couples would gain only £1.35 per week because of interactions with benefits and tax credits.
claims.quote: Around two-fifths (1.1 million) of eligible in-work couples would only gain £1.35 per week due to these interactions

claims.claim: If a non-working spouse transfers their allowance and then enters employment, their partner's tax liability increases, creating a disincentive to work.
claims.quote: If a non-working spouse transfers their allowance, and then decides to enter employment, their partner's tax liability would increase, effectively taxing every pound earned by the working spouse at the marginal rate of tax

claims.claim: Low take-up of the existing allowance means approximately 2 million eligible couples are already missing out.
claims.quote: the take-up of the current Marriage Allowance has been low, with approximately 2 million eligible couples missing out

verdict.rationale: The policy unambiguously increases take-home pay for eligible couples — moving the transferable allowance from 10% to 25% of the personal allowance lifts the maximum annual saving from £252 to around £1,000 per couple. That is a real, if modest, improvement to household after-tax income for those who qualify and claim. However, eligibility is restricted to couples where one spouse earns below the personal allowance, limiting reach: under the existing (smaller) scheme, only around 3.9 million of 12.4 million married couples currently benefit. The IFS flags that even this enhanced allowance is overshadowed by the broader personal allowance increase proposed alongside it. The gain is further diluted for a significant portion of eligible in-work couples, where interactions with tax credits and benefits mean real gains of just £1.35 per week. There is also a secondary distributional issue: the mechanism creates a re-entry disincentive — a non-working spouse who enters work effectively raises their partner's tax bill, which the House of Commons Library notes is a work disincentive particularly for women. On balance, the policy delivers a clear positive on O11 — more take-home pay for a specific subset of married couples — but the effect is minor in magnitude. The conditionality ('as soon as finances allow') means there is no committed delivery timetable, and historically low take-up of the existing allowance suggests many eligible couples may not claim even if enacted.

verifier.notes: All claims are well-supported by their cited evidence. Tiers are correctly assigned — projected forecasts are not presented as measurable facts. The stated claim accurately reflects the policy text. Magnitude/timing are consistent with the evidence (minor, this-parliament with noted conditionality). The work-disincentive point (E15/E14) is correctly included as a nuance rather than a direction-reversal. The IFS quote (E11) via a vertexai redirect is a slight sourcing concern but not blocking. No party-blind or false-balance issues detected — the verdict judges modelled effect on take-home pay only, without motive-attribution. The direction of 'improves' is justified given the claims predominantly show increased take-home pay for eligible couples, with caveats on reach and magnitude appropriately captured.

evidence.snippet: Reform UK will introduce a UK 25% transferable marriage tax allowance as soon as finances allow, meaning no tax on the first £25,000 of income for either spouse, to make work pay and incentivise people back into the workplace.

The existing Marriage Allowance permits a spouse or civil partner who earns less than the Personal Allowance (currently £12,570 for the 2026/27 tax year) to transfer £1,260 (10% of their Personal Allowance) to their partner, provided the recipient is a basic-rate taxpayer (earning between £12,571 and £50,270 in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland)
This transfer reduces the higher-earner's tax bill by up to £252 per year (20% of £1,260)
Claims can be backdated by up to four tax years, potentially yielding a total of £1,260
Despite its availability, the take-up of the current Marriage Allowance has been low, with approximately 2 million eligible couples missing out
HMRC estimated the allowance cost £580 million in 2021/22, benefiting over 2 million couples
Including the Married Couple's Allowance for older couples, the total cost rises to £700 million annually
**Increase the Personal Allowance:** The individual Personal Allowance would rise from the current £12,570 to £20,000
**Enhanced Transferable Allowance:** The maximum transferable Marriage Allowance rate would increase from 10% to 25% of the Personal Allowance
This would result in a tax saving of up to £1,000 per year for the receiving partner (20% of £5,000), a significant increase from the current £252
The total cost over five years is projected to be £391 billion

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) also highlights that while a "more generous transferable marriage tax allowance" is a notable giveaway, it is "dwarfed in size" by the proposed increase in the Personal Allowance
Under the current system, roughly 3.9 million out of 12.4 million married or civil partnered couples benefit, with around 2.7 million being in-work couples

PolicyEngine's analysis of a 100% transferable allowance (a more extreme version) suggested it would benefit 15% to 20% of the population, with households in the second through fourth income deciles benefiting the most
The House of Commons Library noted that such policies could create a "strong disincentive for women to work"

If a non-working spouse transfers their allowance, and then decides to enter employment, their partner's tax liability would increase, effectively taxing every pound earned by the working spouse at the marginal rate of tax

Research by the IFS from 2017/2018 indicated that work incentives for women fluctuate significantly throughout their lives, heavily influenced by family composition and a partner's earnings, especially for those with lower skills
Around two-fifths (1.1 million) of eligible in-work couples would only gain £1.35 per week due to these interactions
Proponents argue that such allowances "recognise marriage" in the tax system and help lower-income couples
They argue it is "poorly targeted" and "too small to incentivise any change in behaviour" or specifically encourage marriage among new parents
Civitas reported that the government had underspent on the existing Marriage Allowance by £2.4 billion over seven years due to low uptake
They argue this would more effectively counter the "couple penalty," increase marriage rates, and potentially boost births to married couples by 47%

The House of Commons Library has previously highlighted that a fully transferable allowance system could be "administratively complex," requiring tax offices to track small incomes and coordinate tax code changes between spouses
